title.en: Define and use rms current and voltage.

say.en: The mains voltage in your home swings between about plus 325 volt and minus 325 volt, fifty times a second. The 230 volts printed on appliances is its rms value: the steady voltage that would heat a resistor just as much. In this lesson: Describe AC through a resistor.
Define and use rms current and voltage.
Represent AC quantities by phasors.

title.en: AC through a resistor; rms values

body.en: A voltage $v = v_m\sin\omega t$ across a resistor R drives $i = i_m\sin\omega t$ with $i_m = v_m/R$: current and voltage are in phase. The average current over a cycle is zero, but the average power is $\frac12i_m^2R$, because i² is never negative. The rms (effective) current is the steady current giving the same heating: $I = i_m/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707\,i_m$; likewise $V = v_m/\sqrt2$. Then P = VI = I²R, just as for DC. AC meters read *rms values*.
body.kn: ರೋಧಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಪರ್ಯಾಯ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರವಾಹ ಒಂದೇ ಹಂತದಲ್ಲಿರುತ್ತವೆ. ಒಂದು ಆವರ್ತನದ ಸರಾಸರಿ ಪ್ರವಾಹ ಶೂನ್ಯ, ಆದರೆ ಉಷ್ಣ ಶೂನ್ಯವಲ್ಲ. rms ಮೌಲ್ಯ = ಗರಿಷ್ಠ/√2.

points.en: In R: v and i in phase
Average of i over a cycle = 0

narration.en: In a resistor, AC voltage and current are in phase. The average current is zero but the heating is not. The rms value, peak divided by root two, is the DC value that heats equally. Meters show rms values.

title.en: On the board: AC in a resistor; rms values

narration.en: An AC source drives a current through a resistor R: v = v_m sin ωt. The current rises and falls in step with the voltage: in a resistor they are in phase. Over a cycle the average current is zero, but the heating i²R never is: the mean of sin² is one half. So the rms current, which heats like an equal steady current, is i_m/√2; likewise V_rms = v_m/√2. Example: 220 V rms mains peaks at about 311 V; a 100 W bulb on it draws about 0.45 A rms. A phasor is an arrow of length v_m turning at ω; its projection on the vertical axis is the value at that instant.

Over a cycle the average current is zero, but the heating i squaredR never is: the mean of sin squared is one half. A phasor is an arrow of length v m turning at omega; its projection on the vertical axis is the value at that instant.

body.en: A phasor is an arrow of length v_m (or i_m) rotating anticlockwise with angular speed ω. Its projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value v_m sin ωt. *Phasors* let us add alternating voltages of the same frequency like vectors and see phase differences at a glance. For a resistor the V and I phasors point the same way.
body.kn: ಫೇಸರ್ ಎಂದರೆ ω ಕೋನೀಯ ವೇಗದಲ್ಲಿ ತಿರುಗುವ ಬಾಣ; ಅದರ ಲಂಬ ಪ್ರಕ್ಷೇಪ ತಾತ್ಕ್ಷಣಿಕ ಮೌಲ್ಯ ನೀಡುತ್ತದೆ. ರೋಧಕಕ್ಕೆ V ಮತ್ತು I ಫೇಸರ್‌ಗಳು ಒಂದೇ ದಿಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿರುತ್ತವೆ.

problem.en: A bulb is rated 100 W for a 220 V supply. Find its resistance, the peak voltage of the supply and the rms current.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A bulb is rated 100 W for a 220 V supply. Find its resistance, the peak voltage of the supply and the rms current.

say.en: Let us solve this together. A bulb is rated 100 watts for a 220 volts supply. Find its resistance, the peak voltage of the supply and the rms current.
R equals V squared/P equals 220 squared/100 equals 484 ohms.
v m equals the square root of 2 times 220 is approximately 311 volts.
I equals P over V equals 100 over 220 is approximately 0.45 A.
So the answer is 484 ohms; 311 volts; 0.45 A.

problem.en: An alternating current is i = 5 sin(100πt) A. Find its rms value and frequency.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. An alternating current is i = 5 sin(100πt) A. Find its rms value and frequency.

say.en: Let us solve this together. An alternating current is i equals 5 sin100 pi t A. Find its rms value and frequency.
i m equals 5 A, so I equals 5/ the square root of 2 is approximately 3.54 A.
omega equals 100 pi rad s to the power minus 1.
nu equals omega /2 pi equals 50 hertz.
So the answer is 3.54 A; 50 hertz.

homework.en: A 60 W, 230 V bulb runs on the mains. Find its rms current, peak current and resistance.

narration.en: Recap. In a resistor, v and i are in phase. rms = peak/√2; meters read rms values. Average power in R: P = V_rms I_rms = I²R. Phasors are rotating arrows; their projections give instantaneous values.
